beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- ask shown answered; no self-intro here (see B00B)
beats.narration_text: I asked Claude to help me think about a simple question -- what happens to a kid who gets stuck on math, and has no one to ask?

props.command:
claude "help me understand what AI tutoring could mean
  for a kid who has no one to ask for help"
output: extra help, out of reach for many

beats.role_note: presenter intro -- 'Hi, I'm Agrima' + lead-in; doubles as the EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY beat
beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Agrima. Today I want to talk about AI tutoring, and what it could mean for kids who have never had extra help. I'll share the hopeful parts, and the cautions too.
beats.visual_intent: presenter card: name, then a short lead-in

beats.role_note: a kid stuck on math: with help they get unstuck; with no one to ask they fall behind and decide they are bad at math -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Picture a kid stuck on a math problem. Nobody at home can explain it. If a parent can help, or a family can pay for a tutor, that kid gets unstuck fast. If not, the confusion piles up. One missed lesson becomes a few. After a while, the kid decides they're just bad at math. That's not a lack of ability. It's a lack of help.
beats.visual_intent: a stuck-on-homework scene branching into two paths: help (unstuck) vs no one to ask ("bad at math")

beats.act: BEAT 4 — what the early research shows
beats.role_note: hybrid human+AI tutoring helped; furthest-behind gained most; worked best when tutors not stretched thin; cost via 'one summary reports'; early, not a guarantee -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: What I found was more hopeful than I expected. In one study, students in low-income middle schools got help from human tutors and AI software working together. The kids who were furthest behind seemed to benefit the most. It worked best when each tutor wasn't stretched across too many students. One summary reports this kind of program cost about seven hundred dollars per student a year, compared with around thirty-five hundred to forty-three hundred dollars for traditional intensive tutoring. That's a big difference, if it holds up. These are early results, not a guarantee.
beats.visual_intent: three finding chips + a cost-per-student bar comparison ($700 / $2,500+ / $3,500-$4,300) with 'one summary reports' flags

beats.role_note: a recent university study (2,000+ college students) found slightly lower grades with an AI tutor; adults; researchers noted limits; how a tutor is built and used matters -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: It's also fair to say that not every AI tutor works well. A recent university study with more than two thousand college students found that those given an AI tutor ended up with slightly lower grades. They also used their other course materials less. The researchers pointed out limits to the study, and these were adults, not kids. To me, that doesn't cancel out the good results. It's a reminder that how a tutor is built and used matters just as much as having one.
beats.visual_intent: study card (2,000+ college students) beside a 'what to keep in mind' card

beats.role_note: most promising for kids who would otherwise have no tutor, with a real person nearby; the question is reach and who is beside them -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: So here's where I've landed for now. AI tutoring looks most promising for kids who would otherwise have no tutor at all. Especially when a real person is nearby, like a teacher, a volunteer, or a mentor, to notice when something isn't working. It isn't a replacement for people. It may be a way to stretch the help that caring people can give. For nonprofits and community groups, the best question isn't, can AI teach? It's, can it reach the child who needs it, and who will be there beside them?
beats.visual_intent: a child at a desk with a laptop and a caring adult beside them, the closing question below

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW -- suggested prompt typed in, viewer-addressed, read aloud and discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn -- ask Claude to help you think through one question: if a child near you had no tutor, what would it take for an AI tutor to actually reach them? It's worth a few honest minutes.

claude "if a child near me had no tutor, what would it
  take for an AI tutor to actually reach them?"

beats.role_note: OUTRO LAW -- restate the title, last beat, source citation
beats.narration_text: The tutor they never had. Maybe it can reach them, if someone is there beside them. Sourced from six reports on AI tutoring; full citations in the description.
